content: Alaria esculenta, commonly referred to as dabberlocks, badderlocks, or winged kelp, is an edible species of seaweed. It is traditionally consumed in regions along the coasts of the far northern Atlantic Ocean, including Greenland, Iceland, Scotland, and Ireland. This seaweed can be eaten either fresh or cooked. Among the twelve species of Alaria found in the British Isles, Alaria esculenta is one of them. This species can grow up to a maximum length of 2 meters. Its frond is characterized by a distinct midrib, with wavy, membranous lamina extending up to 7 cm wide on either side. The frond is unbranched and tapers towards its end. At its base, the plant has a short stipe that arises from a rhizoidal holdfast. The stipe may also bear several club-shaped sporophylls, which can grow up to 20 cm in length and 5 cm in width. The entire frond is brown in color. The stipe, which is short and cylindrical, attaches to rocks via a holdfast composed of branching, root-like rhizoids. The stipe extends into the frond, forming a prominent midrib. The lamina is thin, membranous, and has a wavy margin. In terms of distribution and ecology, Alaria esculenta is widely found in the British Isles, except for the southern and eastern regions of England. It attaches to rocks just below the low-water mark within the Laminaria belt and is frequently found on rocky shores in exposed locations. Leaf-like sporophylls develop from the stipe and are responsible for producing zoospores. Globally, Alaria esculenta is distributed across various regions. In Europe, it is found in Greenland, Iceland, the Faroe Islands, Norway, France, Helgoland, and the Netherlands. In North America, it is present in Alaska, Labrador, and Massachusetts.
